interactions.label: Which bedside finding most reliably distinguishes inflammatory arthritis from de

params.question: Which bedside finding most reliably distinguishes inflammatory arthritis from degenerative osteoarthritis?

answers.text: Morning stiffness lasting more than 60 minutes that improves with activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Inflammatory stiffness lasts over 60 minutes because fluid gels in the inflamed joint overnight, and it eases with movement as blood flow clears inflammatory mediators. Degenerative stiffness clears within 30 minutes.

answers.text: Joint pain that worsens progressively through the day with use

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pattern — pain worsening with activity — is characteristic of degenerative osteoarthritis, where mechanical wear on damaged cartilage causes increasing discomfort throughout the day.

answers.text: Bony enlargement of the distal interphalangeal joints

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bony DIP enlargement (Heberden's nodes) is a hallmark of osteoarthritis, not inflammatory arthritis. Inflammatory conditions like RA typically spare the DIP joints.

answers.text: Crepitus felt on passive movement of the joint

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Crepitus results from roughened cartilage surfaces grinding together and is characteristic of degenerative osteoarthritis, not inflammatory arthritis where the primary pathology is synovial inflammation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinction is morning stiffness duration. Inflammatory stiffness lasts over 60 minutes and improves with activity; degenerative stiffness clears within 30 minutes and worsens with use.
Exactly right. Prolonged morning stiffness (>60 minutes) that improves with activity is the single most useful bedside clue for inflammatory arthritis.

interactions.label: In ankylosing spondylitis, the primary site of inflammation is the synovial memb

params.question: In ankylosing spondylitis, the primary site of inflammation is the synovial membrane, similar to rheumatoid arthritis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is actually false. Ankylosing spondylitis targets the entheses — the sites where tendons and ligaments insert into bone — not the synovial membrane. Enthesitis is the hallmark of spondyloarthropathies, while synovitis is the hallmark of rheumatoid arthritis.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. In ankylosing spondylitis, the primary target is the enthesis (where tendons and ligaments attach to bone), not the synovial membrane. This enthesitis-driven pathology is what distinguishes the spondyloarthropathies from rheumatoid arthritis.

interactions.label: A 45-year-old woman has symmetrical swelling of the MCP and PIP joints, positive

params.question: A 45-year-old woman has symmetrical swelling of the MCP and PIP joints, positive anti-CCP antibodies, and periarticular osteoporosis on X-ray. Which additional joint involvement would make you reconsider a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrist involvement is very common in rheumatoid arthritis. The MCP, PIP, and wrist joints form the classic triad of RA joint involvement.

Correct. RA characteristically spares the DIP joints. DIP arthritis points towards psoriatic arthritis or osteoarthritis instead. This single feature is one of the most reliable ways to differentiate RA from these conditions.
MTP joint involvement is common in RA, particularly early in the disease. A positive squeeze test across the MTP joints is a well-recognised early finding in rheumatoid arthritis.

Atlantoaxial subluxation is a recognised complication of established rheumatoid arthritis due to pannus eroding the transverse ligament of the atlas. Its presence supports, rather than contradicts, an RA diagnosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key point is that RA spares the distal interphalangeal joints. DIP arthritis in a patient otherwise fitting the RA pattern should raise suspicion for psoriatic arthritis or osteoarthritis.
Well done. DIP sparing is a hallmark of rheumatoid arthritis. Finding DIP arthritis should prompt consideration of psoriatic arthritis or osteoarthritis.

interactions.label: Why are disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) like methotrexate essenti

params.question: Why are disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) like methotrexate essential in rheumatoid arthritis, even when NSAIDs adequately control the patient's pain?

answers.text: DMARDs provide more effective and sustained pain relief than NSAIDs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DMARDs are actually slower to act than NSAIDs for symptom relief. Their value lies not in pain control but in halting the immune process that destroys joints.

answers.text: Only DMARDs halt the immune-mediated joint destruction that NSAIDs cannot prevent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do nothing to stop pannus formation and progressive erosion of cartilage and bone. DMARDs target the underlying immune process, actually changing the course of the disease.

answers.text: DMARDs have fewer adverse effects than long-term NSAID therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DMARDs like methotrexate carry significant side effects including hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, and teratogenicity. The reason for their use is disease modification, not a better safety profile.

answers.text: DMARDs correct the underlying HLA-DR4 genetic susceptibility

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DMARDs suppress the immune response but do not alter the patient's genetic makeup (such as HLA-DR4). They control the disease process without curing the underlying susceptibility.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle is that NSAIDs only control symptoms — they cannot prevent the progressive joint destruction driven by immune-mediated inflammation. Only DMARDs halt this process.
Exactly. The critical distinction is that DMARDs modify disease progression by targeting the immune process, while NSAIDs only mask symptoms without preventing joint damage.

interactions.label: A 38-year-old man presents with sausage-shaped swelling (dactylitis) of his righ

params.question: A 38-year-old man presents with sausage-shaped swelling (dactylitis) of his right index finger and arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joints bilaterally. He also has scaly plaques on his elbows. Which diagnosis do these findings most strongly support?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: RA spares the DIP joints and does not cause dactylitis. The symmetrical small-joint pattern of RA affects MCP and PIP joints, making this presentation inconsistent with RA.

Ankylosing spondylitis primarily affects the axial skeleton (sacroiliac joints and spine), not the DIP joints of the hands. Combined with skin psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis is the specific diagnosis.
Correct. DIP arthritis and dactylitis (sausage digit) are essentially pathognomonic for psoriatic arthritis and never occur in rheumatoid arthritis. The scaly plaques confirm coexisting psoriasis.

Gout typically presents as acute monoarthritis, most commonly at the first metatarsophalangeal joint, with crystal deposition. It does not produce the pattern of DIP arthritis with dactylitis seen here.

overallFeedback.feedback: DIP arthritis and dactylitis (sausage-shaped digit swelling) are pathognomonic for psoriatic arthritis. These features never occur in rheumatoid arthritis and are the most reliable bedside clues for differentiating PsA.
Well done. DIP joint involvement and dactylitis are the two anchor features that reliably identify psoriatic arthritis and distinguish it from both RA and AS.
